#76204. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (765 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Sources indicate that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Upcoming York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Sources indicate that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

Recent findings suggest that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an vital question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

According to recent reports, today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

It has been revealed that for these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

Industry observers note that when a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

According to recent reports, at The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

According to recent reports, invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The home where Woodrow Wilson lives as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” states listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

According to recent reports, the estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell says the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

Sources indicate that the three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with fresh matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell says.

Industry observers note that of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

“This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a new home,” Blackwell says. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury organization Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Recent findings suggest that per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

In a recent development, this is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

It has been revealed that evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the company is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

It has been revealed that for reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

Recent findings suggest that the recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 14, Evernorth declared collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

It has been revealed that the storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

Recent findings suggest that “When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane stated.

Delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the company’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.).

The way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

It has been revealed that “The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane mentioned. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners rapidly.”.

According to recent reports, DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane noted.

The performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this company to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane remarked.

Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year.
  • Recent findings suggest that the October jobs report indicated employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace.
  • Industry observers note that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the October jobs report indicated employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Industry observers note that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

According to recent reports, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh noted in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Sources indicate that adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS noted a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

Sources indicate that the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

According to recent reports, forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

Industry observers note that the October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

It has been revealed that bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, reveals that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

Bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

Seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a new position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

According to recent reports, the crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

It has been revealed that goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter demonstrated no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

Industry observers note that besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

A 13F filing only shows long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

#76198. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Sources indicate that investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • In a recent development, access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Sources indicate that investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

In a recent development, access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely indicates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

It has been revealed that one had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

It has been revealed that some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the organization can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Industry observers note that real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

According to recent reports, in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

It has been revealed that if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Industry observers note that say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Recent findings suggest that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

Sources indicate that how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Recent findings suggest that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The firm running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

Recent findings suggest that how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Recent findings suggest that many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

According to recent reports, how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Recent findings suggest that commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your initiative, not the floor under it.

According to recent reports, the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz said that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in Latest York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

Industry observers note that "Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz remarked.

In a recent development, his gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

Industry observers note that A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he noted.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

Sources indicate that "Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz stated, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

Sources indicate that "The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he noted.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

In a recent development, he noted that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he said in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

In a recent development, "First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he stated.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he stated.

In particular, Novogratz said that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

Sources indicate that "Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he noted.

He also noted that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

According to recent reports, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

According to recent reports, the organization confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it indicates can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Recent findings suggest that sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

It has been revealed that “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it stated already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the manufacturer.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Recent findings suggest that compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the organization’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

Recent findings suggest that the dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS confirmed intends for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton stated the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The organization did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

According to recent reports, below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson, there is plenty more to come for Cardano, as the blockchain's privacy-preserving sister chain, Midnight, reaches a huge milestone as its ecosystem continues to expand.

Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.

Industry observers note that "I never once stated Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov. 15 post on X.

The comments came after he talked about the completion of Cardano's original roadmap, which raised some questions about his role in the blockchain's future.

He also called out the CEO of the Cardano Foundation, Frederik Gregaard, for not mentioning the Midnight chain when discussing everything the network has accomplished.

Sources indicate that in his latest video, uploaded on Nov. 17, Hoskinson celebrated the fact that Midnight had just brought on board its first UK-based banking partner, Monument Bank.

Monument Bank is the first UK bank to offer interest-bearing tokenized retail deposits on a public blockchain, according to an announcement from the Midnight Foundation.

Up to £250 million in customer deposits will be added to Midnight in the first phase, and each tokenized deposit will be backed 1:1 by sterling cash held at the bank.

Monument Bank customers can now earn a fixed 5.2% annual equivalent rate on deposits for 12 months, all without having to deal with cryptocurrencies directly.

Hoskinson was very excited about the scale of the initiative, comparing the planned amount of deposits with the current decentralized finance ecosystem on Cardano.

"It's five times the TVL of Cardano," he mentioned.

The £250 million is the planned initial size of the banking product, not a verified figure for how much is currently deposited on Midnight.

Hoskinson called this one of the most crucial milestones in his career.

"This is just one of the many things to come, but I think it's one of the most significant things of at least my career," he mentioned.

He added that the team behind Midnight had moved the originally scheduled hard fork from December to November to accommodate the technical needs of Monument Bank.

Despite the milestone, Hoskinson emphasized that it's only the first step in a much larger mission: bringing traditional financial assets onto Midnight.

It has been revealed that "This mission is not done if these assets are just strictly staying on Midnight. Needs to be expanded to Web3. But inherit from Midnight in terms of safety, security, privacy, simplicity," he stated.

Sources indicate that hoskinson thinks the main barrier to cryptocurrency adoption is the lack of trust among consumers. He believes that simplifying the user experience without compromising regulatory requirements will allow billions of people to join the blockchain economy.

Sources indicate that hoskinson also shared that there's a big event coming up for the Midnight Foundation on Dec. 15. Developers will showcase future products and technological advancements scheduled for 2027.

Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off.
  • That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation.
  • “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:09 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

In a recent development, inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

“As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”.

It has been revealed that bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, the first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to owners and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

According to recent reports, “Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari noted.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari said.

The scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

“On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari mentioned. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”.

That thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari said.

It has been revealed that bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he said: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly vital as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”.

#76192. Tech Report: Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1143 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, turn closings into case studies.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to initiative. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

In a recent development, for years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

It has been revealed that I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

It has been revealed that not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Industry observers note that before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Recent findings suggest that once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

In a recent development, what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a fresh closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Industry observers note that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, Zcash price indicated a massive rally, rising more than 10%.
  • At press time, ZEC is reading near $961.
  • Despite the rebound, the ZEC remains under pressure from institutional fund withdrawals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, Zcash price indicated a massive rally, rising more than 10%.

At press time, ZEC is reading near $961. The recovery follows a sharp a correction that pushed ZEC toward $860 over the weekend.

Despite the rebound, the ZEC remains under pressure from institutional fund withdrawals.

One of the most notable developments is a Zcash Community Grants (ZCG) vote running from November 16 to November 30.

Community members are considering proposals to change how the grants treasury is managed, including a proposal to transfer 50,000 ZEC into the Network Sustainability Mechanism.

Zcash gained 7.69% on November 4, rising on high expectations surrounding NU7. The upgrade introduces several changes to the network's transaction processing and reward structure.

Sources indicate that as the upgrade went live on November 5, the target block interval went from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. According to the project’s statement, the change makes private payments confirm three times faster.

ZEC recently tested the $860 area before recovering. This level is important because derivatives data previously identified a concentration of leveraged long positions around it.

If Zcash returns to that zone, forced liquidations could amplify volatility. $950 is an initial recovery level, followed by the psychological resistance around $1,000.

However, break below $860 could expose ZEC to selling pressure and further decline.

#76189. Latest Update: Pulley raises $64 million to speed permitting and development

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (626 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Pulley raises $64 million to speed permitting and development

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pulley, a development technology firm that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company announced this week.
  • The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures.
  • Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pulley, a development technology firm that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company announced this week.

The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. Pulley said the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and upcoming products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines.

Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.

It has been revealed that pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The company estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions.

It has been revealed that “The speed at which we build is one of the most important challenges facing America over the next decade,” stated Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”.

Pulley remarked it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The manufacturer reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time.

According to recent reports, pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction plan reviews and coordination with local agencies. The organization also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building intends directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement.

According to recent reports, the company noted customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission.

Recent findings suggest that with the latest funding, Pulley plans to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs.

Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance issues earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during plan check.

In a recent development, lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing rapidly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital intends and delay unit delivery into tight markets.

Tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and new capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private plan review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions.

#76188. Breaking: A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

Breaking: A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he remarked.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Recent findings suggest that sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A massive part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Industry observers note that athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively fresh sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he noted, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move rapidly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré remarked. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that but that can be a long road. Sangaré remarked it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

Sources indicate that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré remarked; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following multiple technical outages at major U.S.
  • In a recent X post, Horsley pointed to the weaknesses of traditional financial systems, especially in the context of the world's growing reliance on technology.
  • "Consider having some stablecoins or crypto just in case.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following multiple technical outages at major U.S. banks that left thousands of people unable to access banking services or make transactions, Bitwise CEO Hunter Horsley has urged Americans to keep some of their funds in crypto or stablecoins as a backup plan.

In a recent X post, Horsley pointed to the weaknesses of traditional financial systems, especially in the context of the world's growing reliance on technology.

"Rolling bank outages in the AI era," he stated.

"Consider having some stablecoins or crypto just in case.".

Large U.S. financial institutions such as JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo experienced widespread complaints about technical outages on Nov. 16.

Customers remarked they were having trouble logging into their online accounts, viewing their balances and conducting transactions.

According to recent reports, according to Fox News, the incident affected some of the biggest banking names in the U.S. Thousands of people reported the matter via the outage-tracking platform Downdetector.

Sources indicate that zelle, a popular payment service that people use in the U.S. to transfer funds between bank accounts, was also reportedly affected.

Sources indicate that as of the evening of Nov. 16, Chase had fixed the technical problem, according to the bank. It remarked transactions were back to normal.

The outage reports initially pointed to multiple banking systems going down at the same time. But further investigation revealed that problems at Chase spilled over into transactions with other banks. However, the Zelle app itself continued to work.

Recent findings suggest that stablecoins such as USDT and USDC aim to track the value of the U.S. dollar as closely as possible. They can be an option for those looking to hold digital funds without the extreme price fluctuations of crypto assets like Bitcoin.

In a recent development, for instance, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, participants in blockchain networks can transfer dollar-based stablecoins 24/7. However, cashing them out into traditional money may still require access to traditional financial institutions.

Equifax cuts database firefighting after moving billing to Oracle on AWS

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A multicloud strategy once meant deciding which workloads lived with which provider.
  • The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.
  • “Their performance optimizer is so advanced that we don’t need to tune a single query,” Singh remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:53 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

A multicloud strategy once meant deciding which workloads lived with which provider. Now database providers are moving into the clouds customers already use, and AI projects are raising the value of those migrations well beyond the back office.

Equifax Inc. is a case in point. The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.

“Their performance optimizer is so advanced that we don’t need to tune a single query,” Singh remarked. “Just think about that. Fifteen to 20 tickets per day turns into one to two tickets per month.”.

Recent findings suggest that singh spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how a multicloud strategy is helping Equifax cut billing database tickets. (* Disclosure below.).

According to recent reports, equifax’s global billing system runs on Oracle’s billing and revenue management software, rating and invoicing billions of transactions each month. The database behind it ran on Amazon Relational Database Service for Oracle until it hit a 65-terabyte ceiling. Oracle Autonomous AI Database on AWS, built on Exadata hardware, has room for petabytes of data inside the same cloud, as enterprise adoption accelerates. Because the application stack stayed on AWS, only the database service changed, Singh explained.

“There is zero code writing because it is just about migrating the data from one database to another,” Singh stated. “We achieved this migration without any downtime.”.

The results highlighted up promptly after the system went live in April. Gathering database statistics on nearly 100 terabytes of data dropped from three to four days to three to four hours. After some configuration tuning, batch jobs that once handled 100 to 200 rows per transaction now process 15,000 to 30,000, according to Singh.

“Our rating improved almost 200% to 300%,” Singh noted. “We are able to close our books way before what we have been closing.”.

It has been revealed that bitcoin ETF outflows accelerated as Wall Street extended its losing streak, with Asia’s semiconductor markets suffering their worst weekly declines in decades. Anthropic’s record-breaking $81 billion IPO failed to restore tech stocks. Nvidia also continued falling despite reporting another quarter of extraordinary growth.

US stocks suffered a selloff last night, with the S&P 500 dropping 2.02% to 7,175.83. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%, while the Dow Jones fell 2.19%. More than 90% of S&P 500 companies finished lower.

According to recent reports, the losses extended a six-session losing streak for the S&P 500, its longest since 2024. The index now sits 8.2% below its October record. Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut started with its shares jumping as high as $115 against an $83 IPO price, but the excitement faded swiftly, with shares closing at $97.17.

Nvidia’s latest results should have given investors plenty of reasons to remain optimistic, yet its shares continued falling as Wall Street questioned the sustainability of the AI investment boom. Jensen Huang’s sudden departure was just one layer of uncertainty.

The company reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year. Data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, displaying a huge demand for its AI processors. Nvidia also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. Yet its shares dropped another 3.3% at the market close, extending their losing streak to six sessions.

It has been revealed that the financial commitments behind the AI boom are also attracting greater scrutiny. Major technology companies are increasingly relying on debt markets to finance infrastructure expansion.

The European Central Bank’s November Financial Stability Review underscored growing interconnections between AI companies, including circular financing arrangements. It also warned that changing expectations around AI profitability are triggering a sharp repricing across financial markets.

With US hyperscalers planning enormous infrastructure investments, investors are becoming less willing to accept expensive valuations without clearer evidence of future returns.

Taiwan’s benchmark plunged 17.5% for the week, its steepest weekly decline since 1990. Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s KOSPI recorded weekly losses of 8%. The selling also hit some of the industry’s biggest AI suppliers, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Tech giant, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Recent findings suggest that the concentration of losses across these markets demonstrates how deeply the AI boom has become embedded in global equities. Taiwan supplies advanced chips, South Korea dominates critical memory production, and Japan remains an notable supplier of semiconductor equipment and materials.

A slowdown in AI infrastructure spending is affecting companies across the entire supply chain, not just American technology giants.

According to recent reports, US spot Bitcoin ETFs are still recording heavy outflows. Another $306.5 million in net outflows yesterday, with seven finalized trading sessions producing $1.4 billion in withdrawals.

Sources indicate that bitcoin ETF outflows now coincide with a reassessment of expensive growth assets, weakening institutional demand just as the crypto market faces additional selling pressure. The AI boom has not disappeared, and Nvidia’s latest results demonstrate that demand remains enormous. But investors are no longer rewarding growth at any price.

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is signaling a strategic shift in priorities, moving from building the network’s infrastructure to developing products and driving adoption across its extensive ecosystem, with Midnight (NIGHT) at the epicenter.

On a recent podcast, Hoskinson stated, “Now I’m going from building Cardano to building on Cardano.”.

As pointed out by Cardanians, an educational platform focused on Cardano, Hoskinson described Midnight as the vanguard of this upcoming direction, calling it one of the ecosystem’s most exciting products alongside Midnight City.

More notably, the shift does not mean Cardano’s existing roadmap is being abandoned; rather, Hoskinson suggests the focus is increasingly moving toward delivering practical applications that are instrumental in real-world adoption.

Cardano’s treasury has received 23 million ADA following the return of funds originally allocated to Project Catalyst Fund 15 and Input Output’s Catalyst administration contract.

Cardanians acknowledged that the funds were no longer required since Catalyst administration responsibilities transitioned to the Cardano Foundation.

Their return, therefore, restores previously committed ADA to the treasury, making it available for future ecosystem initiatives and community-approved funding proposals.

This development comes days after the rejection of a proposal seeking 22 million ADA to purchase and tokenize copper, showing the governance community’s ability to vet project funding.

On the price action front, Cardano is nearing a potentially decisive technical level, with Market analyst Lana Valentis highlighting that the cryptocurrency is approaching the midline of a descending channel on the weekly timeframe.

Industry News: West Capital Lending hit with 1099 independent contractor suit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.
  • 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.
