📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.

In a complaint filed Nov. 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.

WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.

According to the complaint, Heaps began working for WCL in November 2023 as a branch manager. In January 2024, he also took on internal technology responsibilities, including customer relationship management (CRM) administration, software development and systems integration. His employment ended in September 2025.

Heaps claims WCL classified him as a 1099 independent contractor while paying him a fixed recurring amount regardless of hours worked and still exercising control over his work. He alleges he reported to a manager, worked from an assigned office in Irvine, did not submit invoices, regularly worked more than 40 hours per week without overtime pay and did not receive his final paycheck after his employment ended.

“This treatment was not merely occasional, but reflected Defendants’ pattern and practice of willfully misclassifying Defendants’ employees as independent contractors,” the lawsuit states.In a statement to HousingWire, Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Michael Sigall, who represent the plaintiff, mentioned they had filed “a class action lawsuit against West Capital Lending, Inc. alleging the company misclassified workers as independent contractors when they should have been treated as employees.”“As a result, workers were allegedly denied basic wage and hour protections California law guarantees. Hardworking people deserve to be paid every dollar they’ve earned, and we are committed to holding West Capital accountable,” they wrote.

WCL, which has about 1,900 sponsored LOs and originated about $10.8 billion year-to-date, has been the target of several lawsuits over its business and employment practices in recent years. Competitors, including loanDepot and Griffin Funding, along with former employees, have filed actions challenging the tech giant’s model. WCL has denied wrongdoing in those cases.

In a recent development, the 1099 independent contractor structure is also part of loanDepot’s ongoing lawsuit against WCL. In that case, loanDepot alleged that WCL misclassified about 600 loan officers as independent contractors, paying them on a 1099 basis and avoiding employment-related costs.

“loanDepot’s investigation has revealed that all of its former California loan originators poached by WCL who still hold California licenses to originate loans switched from operating under the standard MLO license issued by the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI), which requires mortgage loan originators to be employees of their sponsoring lender, to a ‘real estate salesperson with MLO endorsement’ license issued by the DRE [Department of Real Estate] after joining WCL,” the loanDepot complaint states.

Industry observers note that the loanDepot complaint alleges that WCL’s California LOs perform exclusively mortgage loan origination duties, not real estate sales activities. WCL allegedly classifies its California originators as independent contractors while treating those in other states as employees. (WCL also sued loanDepot, alleging Truth in Lending Act violations).

California Labor Code Section 2775 codifies the so-called ABC test for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. However, Section 2778(c)(1) excludes qualifying real estate licensees from the ABC test and directs their classification to California Business and Professions Code Section 10032(b).

In a recent development, that provision allows real estate brokers and salespersons to establish their relationship as either employer-employee or independent contractor. For other purposes under the Labor Code, the Borello multifactor test, which is a more flexible, fact-specific analysis, generally applies.Under the ABC test, which applies to most workers, an individual is presumed to be an employee unless the hiring entity establishes all three conditions: The worker is free from the company’s control and direction, both under the contract and in practice; performs work outside the usual course of the company’s business; and is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation or business of the same nature as the work performed.

In the Heaps case, the complaint asserts that WCL’s treatment of the plaintiff “cannot meet any part of the ABC Test and Defendants knew it.”.

Sources indicate that the DFPI referred questions about this licensing and employment model to the DRE, which did not respond to requests for comment. The Department of Industrial Relations, which enforces labor law, also did not respond to questions.

The use of 1099 models for loan originators and branch personnel has become a flashpoint in California, where some lenders argue that compliance-focused firms are at a competitive disadvantage.

Alan Pezeshkian, president of California-based House America Financial, said he is not opposed to 1099 compensation structures in principle but is concerned about inconsistent application of labor and tax standards.

It has been revealed that “When companies gain a competitive advantage by circumventing employment and tax laws, it creates an uneven playing field and penalizes those of us who make compliance a priority,” Pezeshkian said. “Let’s call it what it is: when a firm improperly classifies employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes and other employment obligations, that’s not innovation, that’s just gaming the system. And when that becomes a recruiting strategy, companies that follow the rules are effectively being punished for doing the right thing.”.

Troy Garris, co-managing partner at Garris Horn LLP, said the inquiry under many laws focuses on control versus independence.

Recent findings suggest that “Under many laws, a worker is an employee if the business can dictate not just what is done, but how, when and where it is done, and by whom. Independent contractors, by contrast, run their own businesses: they set their own methods, use their own tools, take on the risk of profit or loss, and are free to work for other companies,” Garris said. “Some laws make proving contractor status especially difficult, such as under California’s ABC test.”.

Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson, said hiring 1099 independent contractors, from a regulatory perspective, is a “dangerous game” because the definition of “employee” touches multiple regimes.

In a recent development, “Regulation Z does not define employees,” Selden remarked. “If a term is not defined within the regulation, you look to the contract and state law. So, then that’s gray.”Patch: This story has been updated to include a statement from the plaintiff’s attorneys.

#76179. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (822 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

According to recent reports, A sold comp tells us where a buyer mentioned yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Sources indicate that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

According to recent reports, one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

According to recent reports, that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

It has been revealed that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Industry observers note that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

According to recent reports, this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

According to recent reports, twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

According to recent reports, sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the organization's selling spree demonstrates no signs of slowing down.
  • Industry observers note that according to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov.
  • The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining company throughout 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the organization's selling spree demonstrates no signs of slowing down.

Industry observers note that according to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov. 18.

The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining company throughout 2026.

Lookonchain estimates that MARA has already sold a staggering 40,581 BTC this year, generating approximately $3.03 billion at an average selling price of $74,446 per coin.

However, it remains unclear whether the latest 366 BTC transfer represents another completed sale or an internal movement of funds.

MARA's aggressive selling strategy is confirmed by its latest quarterly financial disclosures.

According to recent reports, according to its Nov. 9 SEC filing, the tech giant sold approximately 26,984 BTC for $1.9 billion during the first nine months of 2026.

Following the end of September, MARA liquidated another 13,597 BTC at an average price of approximately $81,039, raising an additional $1.1 billion.

These transactions bring its total disclosed Bitcoin sales to 40,581 BTC.

Notably, the firm used $750 million from its latest sales to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.

Interestingly, MARA has explicitly signaled that it intends to continue selling Bitcoin as part of a broader shift in its corporate strategy.

However, it began allowing sales of newly mined Bitcoin in 2025 before expanding the policy in 2026 to include coins already held on its balance sheet.

In its latest shareholder letter, MARA noted it aims to continue monetizing Bitcoin to strengthen its financial flexibility.

The company specifically identified artificial intelligence infrastructure, upcoming convertible debt obligations and potential share repurchases as reasons for building up cash reserves.

The selling comes as MARA faces considerable pressure on its core mining business.

Third-quarter revenue declined 35% year over year to $164.2 million, compared to $252.4 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

Housing groups cheer Senate passage of milestone permitting bill

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.
  • Sources indicate that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation.
  • Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.

Sources indicate that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation. It is likely one of the last bipartisan measures this Congress will vote on before the 120th Congress is sworn in shortly after the upcoming year.

Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.

Recent findings suggest that BAAJA now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives, which is widely expected to vote on the measure before the newly introduced Congress is sworn in on January 3. However, the clock is ticking, as the House is already on Thanksgiving recess. That leaves about a month for the House to either pass the Senate’s version or reconcile any differences between the two chambers.

If the bill doesn’t reach President Trump’s desk by January 3, the process would have to start over with the fresh Congress, which would likely change some of its provisions.

Many affordable and multifamily projects that rely on federal funding or assistance face regulatory hurdles that most privately financed housing developments avoid.

Industry observers note that these projects include those backed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Examples include housing built using public housing assistance, Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding, USDA housing loans, disaster relief funds and more.

Most notably, these federally backed housing projects must go through National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that don’t apply to most private- sector development projects.

These reviews, critics argue, add an extra regulatory burden that can increase project timelines by a year or more. Critics further contend that NEPA and NHPA, while well-intentioned laws, are often used by NIMBY groups to delay or kill affordable housing development.

In response to these concerns, BAAJA would streamline NEPA reviews for housing development by:.

These changes would strengthen and expand provisions in the HOME Reform Act of 2025, a bill included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that exempted small federal housing projects of 15 units or less from NEPA review.

BAAJA would similarly streamline NHPA reviews and narrow which projects trigger a review, allowing redevelopment projects involving older buildings to move forward more quickly.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, the bill would streamline Clean Water Act reviews, in effect speeding up federal wetlands permitting by shortening review timelines and limiting certain EPA interventions and legal challenges. It would also shorten Endangered Species Act consultation timelines and give states a larger role in federal reviews to reduce permitting delays for residential developments on land with protected species or habitats.

Support for BAAJA spans much of the housing industry. Earlier this month, the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, Up for Growth Action and dozens of other housing organizations and homebuilder groups signed a letter urging the Senate to move the permitting reform package forward.

On Friday, National Association of REALTORS Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said in a statement she supports the legislation’s goal of streamlining “permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction and limit housing supply.”.

“These barriers affect everything from starter homes to multifamily rental housing, making it harder to meet the needs of buyers and renters alike,” McGahn said.

NAHB further argued that BAAJA would reduce land development costs and permitting delays, while also improving multifamily builders’ access to federal housing finance programs. In a statement following the Senate’s vote, NAHB Chairman Bill Owens mentioned that the bill “will help builders deliver the affordable homes families need.”.

Recent findings suggest that “By cutting the regulatory costs and delays that drive up the price of construction, BAAJA will expand housing supply, lower costs for buyers and renters and increase access to affordable rental housing. With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay,” Owens said.

It has been revealed that housing is only a fraction of what BAAJA targets. It mainly aims to streamline the development of a wide range of federally backed projects, including:.

As it does for housing, BAAJA would scale back NEPA and other environmental reviews for these federal projects, while also including other measures to shorten permitting and approval timelines.

In the Senate, 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of the bill.

Senators Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were the only Republican Senators to vote against the legislation, largely because they feared it would undermine states’ rights.

Meanwhile, 31 Democrats voted against it. The legislation has drawn significant opposition from environmental groups concerned that its permitting changes could weaken environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel emissions.

Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, for example, argued that the bill “furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands and endangers wildlife.”.

Other critics of BAAJA worry that the bill’s permitting reforms could accelerate the development of more data centers, including on public lands.

Despite the ongoing opposition from environmental groups, BAAJA has bipartisan support in the House. For example, Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who backs the bill’s permitting provisions, countered these concerns by noting that it would also fast-track renewable energy development. He reiterated his support for the bill after it passed the Senate.

According to recent reports, “BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us,” Peters mentioned in a statement.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont noted in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Industry observers note that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

According to recent reports, “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker remarked workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

According to recent reports, “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

DataBeyond combines AI hyperspectral optical sorting with robotic picking to recover recyclable materials from mixed waste. Optical sorters process high-volume material streams, while robots identify and pick individual recyclable items from complex mixtures. In MSW applications, the company's systems recover target plastics, including polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) films, while separating materials that are incompatible with the intended recycling process. For plastics recycling, DataBeyond offers AI hyperspectral optical sorters that distinguish materials by composition, including plastics with similar appearances. Applications cover mixed rigid plastics, PET bottles and PET flakes. It also supports local operators through system integration, technical training and maintenance services, adapting sorting solutions to local waste composition, infrastructure and recycling markets.

Through these efforts, DataBeyond aims to connect recovery businesses with manufacturers seeking recycled feedstock, helping more recovered materials meet production requirements and return to supply chains.

Founded in 2018, Hangzhou DataBeyond Technology Co., Ltd. develops intelligent waste-sorting equipment and integrated solutions using AI, optical sensing and robotics. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:28 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most important open question in mathematics.

It has been revealed that levent Alpöge confirmed his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The company floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion.

It has been revealed that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”.

The Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects.

The Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral.

It has been revealed that the Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½.

It has been revealed that the hypothesis is considered to be the most crucial open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern.

In a recent development, another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well.

Alpöge wrote that Claude proved not only the standard version of the Riemann hypothesis but also the so-called generalized variant. The latter conjecture argues that the Riemann hypothesis holds true for not only the Riemann zeta function but also certain other, similar functions. Alpöge believes that Claude will be capable of proving an even broader version of the hypothesis in the future.

In a recent development, the researcher detailed that Claude’s proof runs for more than 250,000 pages. He has not yet released the paper. He did, however, publish a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used to verify mathematical results. The file contains millions of lines of code.

It has been revealed that proofs implemented in Lean are essentially regular software programs. If a Lean program runs without crashing, the mathematical argument that it describes is correct. That makes it easier for mathematicians to verify newly published proofs.

Tech Report: Lock-in effect likely to keep HELOCs, second lien activity up through 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan.
  • Annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

Recent findings suggest that according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

Annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve Bank of Latest York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

As a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he noted.

Stratis stated the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

“Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis noted. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

Matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

Recent findings suggest that “Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon said. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a new roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

Industry observers note that tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his organization has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

Recent findings suggest that hutchens mentioned borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

“Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, said that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

Recent findings suggest that “[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz said. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a new loan, he said. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, mentioned borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

“The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen noted. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the latest rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

According to recent reports, leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he mentioned, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

According to recent reports, for borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz said.

Sources indicate that adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, said home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a latest mortgage.

“A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson said. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

Industry observers note that MEXC confirmed that its Global Card service will be discontinued on November 18, according to the exchange's announcement. The company cites service adjustments by its third-party card issuer. From the deadline, existing cards can no longer be used for transactions, and newly introduced card applications are suspended.

Users have two things to take care of before the service ends.

First, the remaining card balance has to be withdrawn: the Withdraw button on the Global Card page sends the funds to the Fiat account.

Second, subscriptions linked to the card should be cancelled or switched to another payment method. Unfortunately for cardholders, recurring payments will most likely fail if they stay on the old card.

If there's still a balance when the service ends, MEXC will credit it to the Spot account, so consumers will simply receive their funds back. It's crucial to keep in mind that pending card transactions need time to settle, which is why the balance snapshot comes on November 21, three days after the shutdown. The amount will be credited within three business days of the snapshot. Users do not need to take any action.

Refunds for previous card transactions will be credited to the Fiat account once MEXC receives them. Pending cashback will be credited automatically as scheduled. Elite VVIP users with zero-fee benefits will be refunded too, though the eligible fees return to their Spot accounts only before December 15.

Transaction history, card orders and cashback records stay available on the Global Card page for three months after the service ends, so it's worth saving anything needed before access ends.

In a recent development, cryptocurrency services delegate certain types of services to third parties all the time, so witnessing a similar situation is more than a possibility here. Realistically, the shutdown is somewhat inconvenient rather than dangerous, as the balances are returned automatically. For owners: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bronx real estate broker Marcia Campbell was arrested and indicted for allegedly failing to disclose felony convictions and pending criminal charges when she applied to renew her Newly introduced York real estate broker license, New York Attorney General Letitia James confirmed Thursday.

In a recent development, campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc. in the Bronx, is accused of falsely stating on a June 2026 renewal application that she had not been convicted of a crime and had no criminal charges pending since her previous renewal, according to the announcement from the Office of the Attorney General (OAG).

State regulators say that during that June 14, 2024, to June 13, 2026, period, Campbell had in fact pleaded guilty to two felonies in Westchester County and was facing 18 pending charges in Bronx County tied to alleged deed theft and real estate investment scams. Once the New York Department of State (DOS) discovered the alleged false statements, her broker license was administratively suspended.

It has been revealed that the case underscores how aggressively New York regulators and prosecutors are now scrutinizing license applications and renewals for real estate professionals, particularly in deed theft and fraud matters. For brokers and agents, the case is a reminder that criminal history disclosures on licensing forms are not procedural formalities, but sworn statements that can carry separate felony exposure if falsified.

The new indictment builds on a series of criminal matters involving Campbell in multiple counties.

In October 2024, Attorney General James and Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark revealed two separate indictments against Campbell. In the first, she and her co-conspirators — including her husband — were charged in an alleged deed theft scheme involving the childhood home of a Bronx woman. Prosecutors say the group gained the homeowner’s trust, then used fraudulent contracts bearing the homeowner’s forged signature to transfer the property to a shell company they controlled and to obtain a $493,500 mortgage on the home. Campbell is scheduled to go to trial in that case on Feb. 22, 2027.

Sources indicate that the second Bronx indictment accused Campbell of running a series of real estate investment scams. According to prosecutors, she induced clients to send her funds for purported real estate transactions, then kept the money and refused to return most of it. Those alleged scams took more than $250,000 from vulnerable Newly introduced Yorkers, including first-time homebuyers, immigrants and a personal friend, the OAG said. A trial date in those cases has not yet been set.

Separate Westchester County prosecutions led to criminal convictions. On Dec. 18, 2025, Campbell pleaded guilty in two cases to Falsifying Business Records in the First Degree and Repeated Failure to File Corporate Taxes, both class E felonies. Authorities remarked those cases involved an alleged deed theft scheme that targeted three Westchester homes and involved roughly $2 million in fraudulently obtained loans. Campbell was sentenced to time served in those matters.

According to recent reports, despite those developments, prosecutors say Campbell submitted a broker license renewal application to DOS in June 2026 covering the period from June 15, 2026, through June 13, 2028. On that application, she allegedly answered “no” to questions asking whether she had been convicted of a crime or had criminal charges pending during the prior licensing period.

Attorney General James alleges Campbell knowingly omitted her December 2025 felony convictions in Westchester County and the 18 Bronx County charges that were already pending at the time she filed the renewal. When DOS identified the discrepancies and referred the matter to law enforcement, the agency suspended Campbell’s license.

Sources indicate that for brokerages, the case highlights the operational risk of failing to monitor the criminal and regulatory status of principal brokers and associated licensees. A suspended or revoked license can jeopardize transactions, commissions and firm reputation, especially in markets where deed theft has drawn heightened scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators.

According to recent reports, new York officials at the state and local level have invested significant resources into deed theft enforcement in recent years, particularly in New York City and surrounding counties where equity-rich but cash-poor homeowners are frequent targets. These schemes often rely on trusted intermediaries, including licensed real estate professionals, to gain access to property records and homeowners.

“Upcoming Yorkers depend on real estate brokers to help them make some of the most vital purchases of their lives,” Attorney General James stated in the announcement, adding that Campbell allegedly abused her role “to steal New Yorkers’ homes and savings, then tried to hide her crimes to maintain her license.”.

Sources indicate that for compliance officers at brokerages and franchisors, the case signals that state regulators are willing to cross-check licensing records with court and tax data and to bring independent criminal charges based solely on false or incomplete filings. Firms may want to revisit internal policies requiring prompt disclosure of arrests and convictions by licensed personnel and procedures for verifying those disclosures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Wimbrow is leaving her role as director of stakeholder relations at the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) after about 20 months to become a vice president at Federal Hall Policy Advisors, she told HousingWire.

Wimbrow, a former FHFA Director Bill Pulte aide, is joining the private sector. POLITICO first reported on her transition. FHFA did not immediately respond to a request for comments.

Sources indicate that “I had a great experience at FHFA. It gave me firsthand understanding of the housing finance system and the policy making process, and the importance of the relationship between the government and the agency,” Wimbrow stated. “My role there was stakeholder relations. So I had a great opportunity to engage with the industry and work with folks in the housing space.”.

During her tenure, Wimbrow stated key discussions with industry participants focused on affordability, credit score modernization, oversight of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and the future of the housing finance system, as well as insurance modernization.

“The industry was very positive with the engagement, and they appreciated the focus of making housing affordable,” she noted.

Wimbrow framed the career move as a natural shift from public service to advisory work.

“I wanted to take what I learned on the agency side, particularly in stakeholder relations and industry engagement, and apply that experience in the private sector,” Wimbrow said. “It’s a natural step for me to decide on Fed Hall; they lobbied me, and they’re the best in the business.”.

Before joining FHFA, Wimbrow spent three years at the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), most recently as director of Build-PAC, NAHB’s bipartisan political arm focused on federal campaigns.

#76165. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Upcoming York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He stated he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

Sources indicate that his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be remarked for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

Sources indicate that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan noted. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he mentioned. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sources indicate that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s right now listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

According to recent reports, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

According to recent reports, natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she noted, but it revealed cold.

It has been revealed that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova noted. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Sources indicate that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Recent findings suggest that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova remarked. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

It has been revealed that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

In a recent development, rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

According to recent reports, “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer mentioned. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Industry observers note that shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Recent findings suggest that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Industry observers note that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein stated.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share fresh songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

In a recent development, on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Recent findings suggest that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Sources indicate that kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova stated she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

Cardano-based stablecoin DJED has announced its sunset, as DJED and SHEN services will wind down on December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC.

DJED represents a crypto-backed, overcollateralized stablecoin protocol on Cardano whose US-dollar peg is maintained algorithmically against an ADA reserve (with SHEN as the reserve coin), rather than by fiat reserves.

"DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC," a DJED-focused X account wrote.

In a recent development, ATTN: DJED & SHEN Holders DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026 at 11:59pm UTC. Please redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN you hold before then. All redemptions are subject to the reserve ratio.

Industry observers note that consumers are urged to redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN they hold before this deadline. Users are to redeem on the protocol and convert their DJED and SHEN back to ADA on the official Djed page. Users who hold DJED or SHEN in liquidity pools, lending markets, or other DeFi platforms are urged to withdraw those positions first, then redeem or swap.

The Djed team noted all systems are fully operational and redemptions are now open, subject to the reserve ratio. It further added that the Djed protocol will be maintained and remain available until December 31, 2026. After this date, all remaining funds will be allocated to the outstanding DJED/SHEN holders once the wind-down is complete.

Djed’s shutdown comes almost three years after its launch, which came in 2023. The stablecoin was officially rolled out on the Cardano mainnet on January 31, 2023, and was developed by COTI in collaboration with the Cardano ecosystem to be used on DeFi protocols on Cardano as a stable alternative to volatile cryptocurrencies.

In positive news for the Cardano ecosystem, Monument Bank Limited has debuted tokenized deposits on the Midnight network, marking a milestone for the network and the decentralized finance ecosystem.

At present, Monument is the first UK bank to tokenize retail deposits on a public blockchain, offering clients a 5.2% AER fixed-term return on savings directly through its existing banking app, delivering institutional onchain finance through a familiar and user-friendly banking experience.

Up to £250 million of client deposits will be represented on Midnight in this opening phase, with deposits recorded one-to-one in sterling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.

Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.

Industry observers note that bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month.

Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.”.

Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.”.

“It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states.

Sources indicate that according to the complaint, the fee was “wedged”  between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner’s title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose.

Sources indicate that in the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement, the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing.

The suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco noted she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future.

Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the lawsuit.

The complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee.

Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center, claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year.

Just a week after Binance suffered the biggest cyberattack seen in the history of the crypto market, the onchain monitoring platform Whale Alert has spotted the hacker moving some of the funds in large quantities.

The transfer has raised concerns across the crypto community about what the hacker might be up to and about the possibility of Binance recovering the stolen funds, especially after they are moved to another wallet.

Although the source did not provide sufficient details about the highly concerning transfer, it indicated that the attacker behind the 2026 Binance hack moved 60,000 ETH on Wednesday in 2026.

The broader crypto market has continued to suffer extreme volatility since the attack happened in late October. Hence, the total portion of Ethereum tokens transferred from the stolen stash is now worth $108.78 million at ETH’s current market price.

While the reason behind the sudden move after a few weeks of silence remains uncertain, further data indicated that the assets were moved in five separate transfers of 12,000 ETH each.

Notably, each transaction was worth between $21.75 million and $21.77 million, and they were identified as Binance’s stolen funds because they were all moved from a wallet labeled 'Binance hack' in 2026.

Considering the history of the transferred funds, the move has sparked speculation that the hacker might already be preparing to spend the stolen funds, further sabotaging Binance’s chances of full recovery.

However, it is notable to note that there is no evidence that the attacker has sold the Ethereum, as the receiving wallet has not been identified.

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AIPro, an AI video analytics tech giant, has released a free version of VistaPro, its fire and smoke detection monitoring software. The release allows facility operators to use basic functions with their existing CCTV cameras and PCs, confirm whether the software suits their actual site, and then add features as needed.

The free version can be downloaded from the AIPro official website (www.aipro.ai/download) without registration or login. The basic functions provided free of charge have no usage time limit. People connect existing CCTV cameras that support RTSP video streaming to an Intel-based Windows PC that meets the recommended specifications, and the software runs without a separate high-performance graphics card.

In a recent development, the free version supports a total of three channels: one AI fire detection channel and two general monitoring channels. The fire detection channel analyzes flames and smoke, and video from multiple cameras can be viewed on a single screen. Detection history, statistics, and automatic reporting are also provided.

According to recent reports, real-time video analysis is performed on the user's PC. Both the free version (Free) and the paid Pro blueprint require an internet connection for updates and version management. Before installation, users can check the recommended PC specifications and CCTV integration requirements on the website.

The free distribution is designed so that users can verify CCTV compatibility and fire and smoke detection in their actual operating environment, and determine the features and operating scale their facilities need.

Recent findings suggest that AIPro recommends first trying the software in a single area where fire risk needs to be monitored. Because camera angles, lighting, and work conditions differ from site to site, the firm explained that it is vital to review detection results at different times of day and decide on the operating approach accordingly. AI analysis results are used by managers to judge on-site conditions and the need for a response.

It has been revealed that real-time alerts, email notifications, and fire and map-based monitoring are provided in the paid Pro initiative. AI detection channels can be added as needed, and a Business plan is available for companies and organizations that operate more cameras or need closed-network or site-specific configurations. Users start with the basic functions and then choose whether to expand according to their operating scale and purpose.

AIPro is an AI video analytics firm founded in 2020 by Professor Cheon-Su Park of Sungkyunkwan University. It has built experience applying video analytics technology in the field for public institutions, including supplying fire and wildfire detection software to the Korea Asset Management Corporation.

AIPro believes that even small stores, warehouses, and workshops can evaluate the feasibility of AI safety management using their existing equipment. Going forward, the tech giant prepares to continue research to enhance fire and smoke detection performance and reduce false alarms, while improving ease of use from installation to reviewing detection results and managing records.
