Homebuilders’ $30B buying spree has cooled; now it’s all execution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for the better part of 15 years, U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals.
  • According to recent reports, yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in revealed deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-tech giant transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed.

It has been revealed that the buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin‘s July acquisition of Holiday Builders, Dream Finders Homes‘ August acquisition of Beazer Homes, and Century Communities’ October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes.

According to recent reports, yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted. Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate.

“We’re not busy now,” one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. “This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing’s happening.”.

It has been revealed that that assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants.

My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing new sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations.

Business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That’s when the industry’s outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how rapidly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy.

Sources indicate that that is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding’s extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households?

It has been revealed that the answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they’ve acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028.

That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins.

Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes.

An attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline.

In a recent development, those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others rapidly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation.

Recent findings suggest that an acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition’s original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive.

Successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered.

That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken.

For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway’s Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity.

Sources indicate that many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built.

It also made strategic sense. Local knowledge, land relationships, management experience, customer trust, and an almost irreplicable entrepreneurial fire and come-what-may resiliency were among the assets the buyers sought to acquire.

Industry observers note that but serving as a benevolent, deep-pocketed, and patient capital-access channel for a local autonomy confederation across an expanding collection of businesses comes at a cost. Separate purchasing organizations, technology systems, back-office functions, product-development practices, and management structures can limit the benefits of larger ownership. When sales are strong and margins are healthy, those costs may be easier to absorb. When sales slow, incentives rise, and profitability contracts, the economics become less forgiving.

It has been revealed that the pressure to coordinate operations, consolidate functions, standardize selected processes, and reduce unnecessary overhead intensifies. So do difficult decisions about regional leadership, divisional responsibilities, and the roles of managers at the divisional and neighborhood level who helped make the acquired businesses successful in the first place.

It has been revealed that those decisions can be disruptive, especially for employees and former owners who believed their companies would continue operating as they had before the acquisition and, in some cases, had enjoyed a solid few-year runway of exactly that. Some will regard the changes as evidence that the fresh parent does not understand the business it acquired. Others will see them as necessary steps toward strengthening the combined organization.

According to recent reports, eliminating management positions or consolidating administrative functions does not, by itself, demonstrate operational improvement. Nor does a departure from established practices necessarily indicate that an acquirer has made a strategic mistake or an unforced error.

The relevant test is whether the changes improve the organization’s ability to develop land, build homes, serve customers, maintain valuable relationships and generate returns that stakeholders and owners can count on as durable. That is a more useful standard than judging an acquisition by how many legacy executives remain in place or by how many familiar operating practices survive.

An crucial distinction exists among the companies driving the latest phase of consolidation. Daiwa House, Sekisui House, Sumitomo Forestry, and Berkshire Hathaway operate with strategic planning horizons and ownership structures that can offer greater flexibility than the quarter-to-quarter performance pressures faced by many publicly traded U.S. homebuilders.

The Japanese companies are publicly traded, and Berkshire Hathaway is accountable to its shareholders. None is insulated from financial performance requirements. But their diversified businesses, substantial resources, and long-term commitments to housing and related industries can allow them to invest in capabilities whose returns may take years to materialize.

So far, that difference has played out as an “acquirer-of-choice” factor as homebuilding firm sellers considered how firms organize and develop the businesses they acquire.

Sources indicate that A longer-term ownership philosophy does not require codifying every management position or maintaining every regional operating structure indefinitely. In fact, patient capital may be most valuable when it enables an organization to undertake difficult transformations without expecting every investment to deliver an immediate earnings benefit.

The challenge is to distinguish costs that can be eliminated from capabilities that need strengthening.

Japan-based companies also have another potentially key advantage. Their experience with industrialized construction, standardized components, manufacturing systems, production engineering and deeply vertical integration extends well beyond what is typical of conventional American site-built homebuilding.

It has been revealed that clayton also brings experience in manufactured housing, factory-based production, and vertically integrated housing-related businesses. Its expanding site-built platform, particularly following the Taylor Morrison acquisition, creates opportunities to combine capabilities that have historically operated in unrelated realms of the residential construction business.

Recent findings suggest that none of this means that industrialized methods developed elsewhere can simply be transplanted into American site-built construction. Differences in building codes, product preferences, transportation, trade labor, land development, and construction practices remain unsolved obstacles.

According to recent reports, the industry has not yet demonstrated that these capabilities can be deployed broadly enough to transform the economics of conventional site-built housing. Still, the long-term strategic opportunity is hard to refute.

A collection of independently operated regional builders can provide market presence, land access, local expertise and “trust capital.” A more coordinated enterprise may also provide the common systems, product architecture, production volumes, and organizational learning needed to adapt industrialized methods across multiple markets.

In a recent development, as ambitions go, that’s far bigger than reducing SG&A. It also raises a question that applies to every major acquirer: Which capabilities should remain local, which should be shared across the enterprise, and which should be fundamentally reengineered into the holistic, interoperable system modern homebuilding organizations seem to need?

Homebuilding has long featured an argument over whether privately held regional builders are inherently better businesses than their larger public competitors. The case for private builders emphasizes their closeness to customers, knowledge of local land markets, relationships with municipalities and trades, and the loyalty and committed engagement of talented employees who have worked together for years.

Industry observers note that those advantages are real in many companies. They can influence everything from land acquisition opportunities to construction execution and customer referrals. But private ownership does not guarantee those qualities, just as public or institutional ownership does not necessarily diminish them.

A privately held company can become inefficient, undercapitalized, or resistant to change. A large enterprise can cultivate strong local leadership, build trusted community relationships, and adopt operating practices that improve the customer experience.

The more useful distinction concerns the quality of the operating organization, a characteristic we’ve talked about as homebuilding’s “outlier” factor.

In a recent development, does it put decisions in the hands of people with the knowledge to make them? Does it give those people the resources, information, and accountability to perform effectively? Can it identify successful practices and extend their benefits beyond the division where they originated?

Answers to those questions reveal more than public or private ownership labels. They also help explain why the integration decisions now confronting the major consolidators are so difficult. An organization can destroy valuable local capabilities by centralizing too much. It can also waste substantial resources and miss opportunities to improve by centralizing too little.

Integration is knowing the difference. Some acquirers are good integrators. That doesn’t mean people swept up in them, or spat out due to them, agree.

For decades, scale in homebuilding has largely meant more closings, more communities, more controlled lots, greater geographic reach, and increased purchasing power that leads to market-share advantages. Those advantages remain as a bulwark of near-flywheel-like value creation. Larger builders can spread fixed costs across more homes, negotiate favorable supplier arrangements, diversify market exposure, and access capital on terms that smaller competitors may struggle to match.

Still, everyone who’s done well in the business can attest that size alone does not explain why some organizations consistently outperform others.

It has been revealed that A more meaningful definition of scale includes an enterprise’s ability to combine capital, land, local knowledge, talent, technology, and relationships into an operating system that continuously improves performance. In that sense, homebuilding was AI before AI was cool because its best operators knew and practiced “recursive learning” as a core skill set.

That means acquiring land at bases that support acceptable returns under realistic demand assumptions. It also means developing products that customers value without unnecessary design, material, or construction complexity.

It means coordinating suppliers and trades to reduce delays, rework, and waste. It also means developing managers who can exercise sound judgment locally while drawing on the organization’s broader capabilities. It also means using information gathered across markets to make better decisions throughout the enterprise.

A builder operating in 20 markets should have opportunities to learn from 20 distinct sets of customers, land conditions, construction challenges, and operating practices. But those opportunities yield little advantage if the information remains trapped within individual divisions or if the organization lacks the discipline to identify and transfer improvements.

This is where AI-powered data systems and other technology capabilities could change the economics of scale. Better demand forecasting, more accurate construction scheduling, earlier detection of cost overruns, improved land underwriting, and more systematic comparisons of product performance could help organizations spot problems sooner and make decisions faster.

It has been revealed that AI could help reveal patterns that managers would otherwise struggle to recognize in large volumes of operational data. It could also make institutional knowledge more accessible to those making daily decisions about land, purchasing, construction, and sales.

Sources indicate that but value will not come from installing technology alone. Companies will need reliable data, consistent definitions, disciplined operating processes, and managers who can distinguish useful insights from misleading conclusions. They will also need to recognize that an approach that works in one market may be a fool’s errand in another.

In a recent development, competitive advantage will belong to organizations that can repeatedly measure performance, understand what drives it, test improvements, and incorporate what they learn into their operating practices. That is how scale becomes a capability rather than merely a measurement of size.

The difficult market conditions facing builders through 2027, and potentially into 2028, will make these distinctions more apparent. Management teams will face pressure to reduce overhead, preserve liquidity, reassess land commitments, control construction costs, and improve returns on capital. Some will need to reorganize divisions, consolidate functions, or change leadership.

Sources indicate that the companies that emerge stronger will not necessarily be the ones that make the deepest cuts. They will be the ones that understand which costs can be eliminated without harming the business and which investments are necessary to improve its future performance. That requires financial discipline, but it also requires patience, sound leadership judgment, and a willingness to challenge established practices.

According to recent reports, it may require replacing an operating system that has worked adequately for years. It may also mean changing the responsibilities of respected executives or asking local teams to adopt practices developed elsewhere in the enterprise.

Sources indicate that it may also require resisting the temptation to standardize activities that rely on local relationships and judgment. The objective should be neither to preserve acquired companies exactly as they were nor to eliminate their differences in pursuit of corporate uniformity.

It should be to develop organizations that can achieve what their constituent businesses could not accomplish independently.

The returns earned by companies that participated in homebuilding’s consolidation era will not reflect the ultimate opportunity. American homebuilding remains a uniquely complex process of converting land, capital, materials, labor, knowledge, and time into a finished product that households can purchase. Every unnecessary delay, redundant process, avoidable error, excessive handoff, and poorly coordinated decision adds cost somewhere along that process.

It has been revealed that some of those costs are so sticky they seem almost unavoidable. Others reflect operating practices that have persisted through the decades because the industry has struggled to coordinate the many participants involved in building a home.

Larger enterprises with better information, stronger leadership, deeper technical capabilities, and greater capacity to invest in improvement can change that.

The goal should be a homebuilding value stream that produces more value with less wasted time, effort, and expense, i.e., less “stream.”.

Sources indicate that better execution will not, by itself, overcome high land prices, expensive financing, restrictive regulation, infrastructure constraints, or the gap between household incomes and housing costs. Those barriers remain substantial. But homebuilders have meaningful control over how they organize their businesses and how efficiently they turn resources into finished homes.

According to recent reports, the industry’s era of consolidation has brought together an enormous collection of land assets, operating organizations, local relationships, and management talent under larger ownership platforms. What happens next will determine whether those combinations yield more than additional market share and purchasing leverage.

The most vital measure of homebuilding’s great acquisition era may ultimately have little to do with how many companies changed hands or how much their buyers paid.

It may be how much better those enterprises become at converting land, capital, talent, and knowledge into homes that more American households can afford.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents mentioned.

Sources indicate that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint stated he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

Industry observers note that white also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or strategy.”.

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

In a recent development, pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears remarked the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

Industry observers note that “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

Three-year committed facility provides MetaOptics with flexible growth capital, drawn down at the Firm's sole discretion.

SINGAPORE, Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MetaOptics Ltd (Catalist: 9MT) (OTCQX: MOTLY) ("MetaOptics" or the "Firm", and together with its subsidiaries, the "Group"), a Singapore-headquartered semiconductor optics company pioneering glass-based metalens solutions enhanced by AI-driven image processing, announced that it had on 20 November 2026, entered into a share subscription facility agreement with GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd. ("GEM"), the Bermuda-based investment vehicle managed by Global Emerging Markets (GEM), New York, for an aggregate commitment of up to S$32 million (the "Share Subscription Facility"). The Share Subscription Facility is subject to, inter alia, the approval of the Company's shareholders ("Shareholders") at an extraordinary general meeting ("EGM") to be convened. A circular containing further details of the Share Subscription Facility, together with the notice of EGM, will be despatched to Shareholders in due course.

The Company intends to apply the net proceeds from drawdowns under the Share Subscription Facility, entirely for the Group's working capital purposes, including general corporate expenses, funding the day-to-day operations of the Group and supporting the growth of its existing business. As part of the Group's prepares to grow its existing business, the Group intends to establish a fresh 12-inch glass semiconductor fabrication line in the United States to produce metalenses for co-packaged optics ("CPO") and colour imaging applications. The Share Subscription Facility provides MetaOptics with flexible access to growth capital while allowing the Company to control the timing of any drawdowns, in line with its capital needs and prevailing market conditions.

Sources indicate that mr Thng Chong Kim, Executive Chairman of MetaOptics, said: "This Share Subscription Facility gives us a reliable, flexible source of capital for our day-to-day operations and to support the growth of our existing business by establishing a newly introduced 12-inch glass semiconductor fabrication line in the United States, on terms that put MetaOptics in control of the timing and size of each drawdown. We are pleased to have the backing of GEM, an experienced global investor, as we execute on our plans and build long-term value for our Shareholders.".

This press release should be read in conjunction with the announcement released by the Company on SGXNet on 23 November 2026 in relation to the Share Subscription Facility.

About MetaOptics LtdMetaOptics Ltd (Catalist: 9MT) is a leading-edge semiconductor optics firm pioneering glass-based metalens solutions enhanced by AI-driven image processing. Using advanced optical design and a scalable 12-inch DUV lithography process, it powers next-generation applications in CPO, mobile, AR/VR, automotive and other emerging markets. Headquartered in Singapore, MetaOptics aims to deliver high-performance optics with the reliability and scalability demanded by today's most innovative technology brands. Find out more at www.metaoptics.sg.

It has been revealed that about GEMGEM (Global Emerging Markets) is a US$3.4 billion alternative investment group with operations in Paris, Latest York, Los Angeles and the Bahamas. GEM manages a diverse set of investment vehicles focused on emerging and developed markets and has completed over 600 transactions in 75 countries. Each investment vehicle has a different degree of operational control, risk-adjusted return and liquidity profile. Its family of funds and investment vehicles provides GEM and its partners with exposure to Small-Mid Cap Management Buyouts, Private Investments in Public Equities and select venture investments. For more information, please visit www.gemny.com.

Forward-Looking StatementsThis press release contains forward-looking statements, including statements regarding the share subscription facility, the Firm's intended use of proceeds and its business prepares. These statements are based on the Company's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. The Facility is subject to shareholder approval at the EGM, and drawdowns under the Facility are subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions and to the execution of definitive documentation. There can be no assurance as to the amount or timing of any funds the Company may ultimately raise. The Company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements except as required by law.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.
  • Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions.
  • “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Noted another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

In a recent development, scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium:.

In a recent development, dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he mentioned during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these latest forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

According to recent reports, the financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

“It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

According to recent reports, the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

It has been revealed that “We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he mentioned during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

Infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

“We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

“You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he said during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

Industry observers note that “What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole company. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

According to recent reports, alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The company’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

“We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

Keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

Sources indicate that “You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he said during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

Sources indicate that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

Recent findings suggest that I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

Oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

In any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we revealed a deal with Iran in June.

In a recent development, I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing concerns, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

For the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates?

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:.

According to recent reports, if all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%.Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed’s hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there?1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable.2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war.3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently.We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher.

Recent findings suggest that mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads’ job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under.

According to recent reports, historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

In a recent development, our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

It has been revealed that we saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today.Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:.

According to recent reports, purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:.

Housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time.

Inventory growth is running at 8.12%.

Fresh listings have been in their seasonal decline since June, and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since early 2022. One concern always with higher rates is that sellers will decide not to put their homes on the market; that has not happened this year, which is a positive sign for housing.In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:.

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point, demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%, and last week the year-over-year price-cut gap was 2% higher than last year when demand was picking up with lower rates.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast is going to have a hard time being right this year. I simply don’t have enough time to be correct, as most of the year prices have been rising roughly 1%-2 % with the Case-Shiller Index. It’s only recently that we can see some negative year-over-year data, and we only have a few weeks left in the year.The price-cut percentage for last week:.

Industry observers note that it’s Thanksgiving week, so this means we can see some crazy volatility with stocks and bonds — and some hours with not a lot of volume. Next week’s tracker will obviously be hit by the holidays. However, this week we do have some economic data that can move the markets. PCE inflation, new home sales, PMI and other reports will add to the mix of volatility. And who knows what “upgrades” might shut down another institution or part of our infrastructure from operating normally this week!

The Single Asset Vault amendment on the XRP Ledger is getting closer to activation on the mainnet as validator support builds for the network’s preparation to enable better DeFi functionality.

In a recent development, according to data from XRPScan, the SingleAssetVault amendment, or XLS-65, has received yes votes from 25 of 35 trusted validators, at the moment standing at 71.43% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of 35 votes (29) to start its 14-day countdown to activation. That means it needs four more votes to get there and could reach the magic number before the end of 2026.

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger’s amendment process requires a proposed amendment to be approved by more than 80% of trusted validators for 14 days before it is implemented. Validator support may shift during this time, and if the required 80% threshold is lost, activation may be delayed.

Sources indicate that the Single Asset Vault amendment creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. The amendment introduces a Vault object that defines the state of a tokenized vault, and the Vault entry is one of the ledger entry types it provides.

The Vault object holds key information such as available assets, shares, total value, and other relevant information. Owners can create a Vault object with the VaultCreate transaction; the Vault object is tracked in an Owner Directory owned by the Vault Owner account.

The XRP Ledger lending amendment has gained additional yes votes. According to XRPScan, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment, also known as XLS-66, has received 24 yes votes out of 35 trusted validators, meaning it has 68.57% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of the 35 votes (29) to trigger a 14-day activation countdown.

This implies that there are five votes left for it to reach this threshold, with the possibility of it securing the required number of votes before the end of 2026 as well.

According to XRP enthusiasts, LendingProtocolV1_1 represents the biggest amendment for unlocking capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger and is anticipated by institutional and retail people.

Recent findings suggest that "The third quarter was a period of adjustment for us," noted Wayne Huang, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Zepp Health. "Tight supply for some of our core products weighed on revenue, while unfavorable exchange rates and higher prices for memory and other chips put pressure on gross margin. The adjustments we made across our products, training software, supply, and retail are already beginning to pay off in the fourth quarter, and we are heading into the holiday season and the year ahead with momentum.

In the third quarter, global activations across the Balance family rose approximately 40% from the second quarter, driven by our new, higher-priced models. Combined global activations for Active 3 Premium and Active Max, our two US$169 models, grew approximately 35% over the same period. We also expanded our premium outdoor lineup with T-Rex Dual Solar, a watch priced at about US$650 that pairs a bright AMOLED display with dual-sided solar charging and offline navigation for multi-day trips. Through Zepp OS 6 and HYROX updates, we brought new training tools to more watches that customers already own, giving them more value from their devices.

It has been revealed that product availability has started to improve in some markets in the fourth quarter, including for T-Rex 3. We have also made it easier for customers to compare watches in stores. At REI, we provided materials to help shoppers compare models. Large screens are now in place at our Amazfit counters in select Best Buy stores. They make the counters easier to spot and show shoppers how our devices fit into everyday activity, training, and recovery. As more products reach store shelves, we believe we will be better positioned to meet holiday demand.".

In a recent development, leon Deng, Chief Financial Officer of Zepp Health, commented, "Third-quarter revenue reached US$68.3 million, up 7.5% sequentially and within our guidance range. While revenue declined 9.9% year-over-year, we continued to see encouraging momentum in our Active series. Supply constraints on certain higher-margin products, including Balance 3 and Helio Strap, limited our ability to fully capture market demand during the quarter.

Gross margin was 35.0%, compared with 37.4% in the previous quarter and 38.2% in the same period last year, reflecting unfavorable foreign exchange movements, continued increases in memory component costs, and supply constraints on our higher-margin products. Importantly, excluding the tariff-related benefit recorded in the second quarter, our underlying gross margin remained strong sequentially. Continued improvement in our product mix helped offset a meaningful portion of these external cost pressures, demonstrating the progress we have made in strengthening our premium product portfolio and underlying unit economics.

It has been revealed that we continued to balance financial discipline with targeted investments to support future growth. On a sequential basis, adjusted operating expenses decreased to US$34.2 million, and adjusted operating loss narrowed to US$10.3 million. The year-over-year increase in operating expenses was primarily driven by strategic investments in upcoming product launches, brand building, athlete partnerships, and distribution expansion. At the same time, general and administrative expenses declined, reflecting our ongoing efforts to improve operational efficiency and manage our structural cost base.

It has been revealed that we ended the quarter with US$99.0 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, while inventory declined to US$68.6 million from US$87.7 million a year earlier. We also continued to strengthen our balance sheet by extending our debt maturity profile, converting an additional US$26.6 million of short-term borrowings into longer-term obligations during the quarter. We remain committed to returning value to shareholders through our ongoing share repurchase program. As of September 30, 2026, we had cumulatively repurchased US$17.8 million under our US$20 million authorization, and our board of directors recently approved a one-year extension of the existing program.

Recent findings suggest that looking ahead, we expect fourth-quarter revenue to be between US$90.0 million and US$95.0 million, representing year-over-year growth of approximately 6% to 12%. As product availability improves and our expanded distribution channels begin contributing more meaningfully, we remain focused on translating our investments into stronger revenue growth and greater operating leverage. Despite near-term external cost pressures, we believe our improving product mix, disciplined cost management, and continued investment in the Amazfit brand are building a stronger foundation for sustainable long-term growth and profitability.".

Third Quarter of 2026 Financial Results.

Sources indicate that revenue reached US$68.3 million, representing a year-over-year decrease of 9.9% and a quarter-over-quarter increase of 7.5%. The year-over-year decline was due to the broader macroeconomic environment and a strong comparison base, as well as supply constraints on top-selling offerings, particularly Helio Strap and Balance 3. However, revenue from the Active series increased significantly year-over-year.

Gross margin was 35.0%, compared with 38.2% and 37.4% in the same period of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. Gross margin faced several headwinds during the quarter, primarily elevated memory and other component costs, as well as foreign currency impacts. While product mix improved year-over-year, supported by upcoming product introductions including the Active series, this favorable mix benefit was more than offset by higher memory costs within our entry-level price segments. Gross margin for the second quarter of 2026 benefited from tariff refunds that the Organization recorded related to duties previously remitted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act ("IEEPA"). Excluding the impact of these refunds, gross margin increased sequentially.

Research and Development Expenses.

Sources indicate that research and development expenses in the third quarter of 2026 were US$11.4 million, compared with US$10.8 million and US$11.5 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. Excluding US$0.6 million of foreign currency headwinds, research and development expenses were flat compared with the same period of 2025. We continued to invest in a series of cutting-edge products as well as upcoming technologies, including AI, to maintain our competitive edge against our peers. At the same time, we focused on refined research and development approaches, consistently evaluating resource efficiency to optimize return on investment and productivity.

Industry observers note that selling and marketing expenses in the third quarter of 2026 were US$18.0 million, compared with US$12.0 million and US$18.3 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. The US$6.0 million year-over-year increase was primarily attributable to US$1.9 million investment across online and offline channels for content refreshes, in-store displays and holiday season readiness, and US$1.5 million of launch campaigns for fresh products including the Balance 3, Balance Ultra and T-Rex Dual Solar. The remainder of the increase reflected US$1.4 million for marathons, Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) and media sponsorships, and US$1.2 million related to the HYROX and new athletes partnerships.

General and Administrative Expenses.

General and administrative expenses were US$5.6 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with US$7.0 million and US$6.2 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. We continued to streamline overhead, maintaining disciplined cost control while improving operating efficiency.

GAAP and adjusted operating expenses[2] for the third quarter of 2026 were US$35.0 million and US$34.2 million, respectively, compared with US$29.8 million and US$28.6 million in the third quarter of 2025, and US$36.0 million and US$34.8 million in the second quarter of 2026. Out of the year-over-year increase of US$5.2 million in operating expenses, US$0.8 million was due to foreign currency impacts. The remaining US$4.4 million was primarily due to higher selling and marketing expenses as mentioned above. On a quarter-over-quarter basis, operating expenses decreased slightly.

In a recent development, GAAP and adjusted operating results[3] were loss of US$11.1 million and loss of US$10.3 million, respectively, compared with loss of US$0.9 million and income of US$0.4 million in the same quarter of 2025. The net operating loss was due to lower gross margin mainly resulting from higher memory and other component costs and foreign currency headwinds, as well as increased investment in marketing and branding activities, but the operating loss narrowed compared with the second quarter of 2026.

Industry observers note that GAAP and adjusted net loss attributable to Zepp for the third quarter of 2026 were US$12.6 million and US$11.6 million, respectively, compared with GAAP and adjusted net loss of US$1.6 million and US$0.7 million for the same quarter in 2025. The US$10.9 million year-over-year increase in adjusted net loss was primarily driven by a US$6.0 million increase in selling and marketing expenses, as discussed above, followed by a US$3.2 million unfavorable foreign exchange impact. In addition, higher memory and other component costs resulted in a net US$2.7 million gross profit headwind, partially mitigated by a more favorable product mix. These unfavorable impacts were partially offset by US$1.1 million in savings from general and administrative expenses.

[2] Adjusted operating expenses represent operating expenses excluding (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. Please refer to the section titled "Reconciliation of GAAP and Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.

Industry observers note that [3] Adjusted operating income/(loss) represents operating income/(loss) excluding: (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. See "Reconciliation of GAAP and Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.

Liquidity and Capital Resources.

As of September 30, 2026, cash and cash equivalents and restricted cash were US$99.0 million, compared with US$102.6 million and US$106.3 million as of September 30, 2025 and June 30, 2026, respectively.

The Company recorded inventory of US$68.6 million as of September 30, 2026, compared with US$62.4 million as of June 30, 2026 and US$87.7 million as of September 30, 2025. We will continue to manage the inventory level tightly and working capital closely.

Long-term and short-term debt levels remained flat as of September 30, 2026 compared with June 30, 2026. We remain committed to prudently managing our debt profile. Our primary objective is to maintain overall debt levels broadly stable while actively extending the maturity profile by replacing short-term borrowings with long-term debt. During the third quarter and for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we successfully converted US$26.6 million and US$56.5 million, respectively, of short-term debt into long-term obligations, and we expect to continue this strategy in the coming quarters, supported by sufficient financial headroom and liquidity capacity. Since the beginning of 2023, the Tech giant has cumulatively retired US$38.1 million of debt, and will continue to optimize its capital structure.

Share Repurchase Program Enhancement.

The Firm announced in its third quarter 2021 earnings release that the board had authorized a share repurchase program of up to US$20 million through November 2022. On November 21, 2022, the board authorized a 12-month extension of the Company's share repurchase program. On November 20, 2023, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 12 months. On November 18, 2024, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 24 months. On November 22, 2026, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 12 months. Pursuant to the extended share repurchase program, the Company may repurchase its shares in the form of ADSs and/or ordinary shares through November 2027 with an aggregate value equal to the remaining balance under the share repurchase program. As of September 30, 2026, the Company had used US$17.8 million to repurchase approximately 2.4 million ADSs. The Company expects to fund the repurchases under the extended share repurchase program out of its existing cash balance.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, the Company's management currently expects net revenues to be between US$90.0 million and US$95.0 million, which would represent an increase by approximately 6% to 12% from US$85.2 million in the fourth quarter of 2025.

This outlook is based on current market conditions and reflects the Company's current and preliminary estimates of market, operating conditions and customer demand, which are all subject to change.

Recent findings suggest that zepp Health (NYSE: ZEPP) is the technology tech giant behind Amazfit, a global sports technology brand. Its wider portfolio includes Zepp Clarity hearing technology and Zepp Aura sleep and recovery services.

The firm's vertically integrated technology platform brings together Zepp OS, wearable chipsets and biometric sensors designed in-house, and algorithms for biometric measurement and personalized guidance to enhance product performance and user experiences across devices, software and services.

Zepp Health operates as a global multi-hub organization, bringing together R&D, product, design, brand and business expertise across the Americas, Europe and Asia. These teams co-create and share responsibility for innovation, product performance and global growth.

Founded in 2013, Zepp Health has shipped more than 200 million units of smart wearable devices, with products available in more than 90 countries. Its principal office is in Gorinchem, the Netherlands. For more information, visit: www.zepp.com.

It has been revealed that we use adjusted net income/(loss), a non-GAAP financial measure, in evaluating our operating results and for financial and operational decision-making purposes. Adjusted operating expenses represent operating expenses excluding (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. Adjusted operating income/(loss) represents operating income/(loss) excluding: (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. Adjusted EBIT represents net income/(loss) excluding (i) share-based compensation expenses, (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements, (iii) gain/(loss) from fair value change of long-term investments, (iv) impairment loss from long-term investments, (v) income/(loss) from equity method investments, (vi) investment income/(loss), (vii) income tax (benefit)/expense, and (viii) interest income and interest expense. Adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation is a non-GAAP measure, which excludes (i) share-based compensation expenses, (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements, (iii) gain/(loss) from fair value change of long-term investments, (iv) impairment loss from long-term investments, (v) income/(loss) from equity method investments, (vi) investment income/(loss), and (vii) tax effects of the above non-GAAP adjustments, and is used as the numerator in computation of adjusted net income/(loss) per share and per ADS attributable to Zepp Health Corporation.

We believe that adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation help identify underlying trends in our business that could otherwise be distorted by the effect of certain expenses that we include in net income/(loss) and net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation. We believe adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation provide useful information about our operating results, enhance the overall understanding of our past performance and future prospects and allow for greater visibility with respect to key metrics used by our management in its financial and operational decision-making.

Sources indicate that adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation, should not be considered in isolation or construed as an alternative to net income/(loss), basic and diluted net income/(loss) per share and per ADS attributable to Zepp Health Corporation or any other measure of performance or as an indicator of our operating performance. Investors are encouraged to review the historical non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. Adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to ordinary shareholders, presented here may not be comparable to similarly titled measures presented by other companies. Other companies may calculate similarly titled measures differently, limiting their usefulness as comparative measures to our data. We encourage investors and others to review our financial information in its entirety and not rely on a single financial measure.

In a recent development, tokenized equities are rapidly becoming a major competitive landscape among blockchain networks. Speaking at the 2026 Breakpoint conference, Raoul Pal praised Solana as the leader in tokenized stock volume, highlighting the network’s immense trading volume.

At the Solana Breakpoint conference this week, the CEO of the Real Vision financial platform recognized the explosive growth of the tokenized stocks market on the SOL network.

The celebrated macro investor said the total value of tokenized equities on Solana has increased from $10 million to over $2 billion in just 15 months. He viewed this massive growth as a strong connection between traditional stock markets and the Solana network.

In recent months, the global tokenized stocks market has delivered notable results on the blockchain infrastructure. According to the latest RWA.xyz report, the global tokenized stock market has reached $3.66 billion, with Solana leading the race in market value, as Raoul noted.

Trading volume in tokenized equities on Solana surged to $2 billion, a 2000% increase from $10 million 15 months ago. This clearly indicates that the network has surpassed its competitors, including BNB Chain and Ethereum, to become the global leader in the tokenized stock market.

Multiple tokenized stock products are already operating on Solana, including those for Johnson & Johnson, Exxon Mobil, Salesforce, Uber, Disney, and several others.

Amid the rapid rise of the tokenized stock market, institutional investor participation is also surging.

Earlier this month, Securitize confirmed the debut of its tokenized stocks on Solana. The move signals that major institutions are turning to blockchain infrastructure to integrate tokenized stocks into supported DeFi services and blockchain applications.

Industry observers note that the integration with Solana means eligible global customers will soon be able to trade Securitize’s tokenized stocks on-chain. This reflects continued institutional interest in Solana as an ecosystem for trading tokenized assets.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that crowdStrike Holdings Inc.
  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
  • It has been revealed that investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Industry observers note that crowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

It has been revealed that investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

In a recent development, software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

It has been revealed that zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a firm’s employees access its business applications.

In a recent development, enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

The firm’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

Recent findings suggest that the potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The company’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity challenges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although XRP has achieved a sharp price rally after the severe price correction seen in the past months, its recent recovery has yet to influence the performance of its ETF market.

Latest data from SoSoValue demonstrates that momentum across the XRP ETF market has remained slow as the funds have continued to post massive withdrawals during each trading session in recent days.

Data reveals that the XRP ETFs managed by Canary Capital and Grayscale recorded combined withdrawals of $6.14 million during their latest trading session on November 17.

This also represents the total daily net outflows recorded on that day as only the two funds were active while the rest of the XRP ETF products remained muted with zero participation from investors.

While this means that investors have continued to withdraw their funds despite XRP attempting to reclaim the $1 price level, Canary Capital's XRP ETF saw the highest withdrawal of the day.

Notably, the fund recorded over 5 million XRP, worth about $5.01 million, in daily outflows, while Grayscale's XRP ETF followed with just $1.12 million in outflows.

Although Bitwise did not record any inflow or outflow on this day, the firm still stands as XRP’s biggest ETF manager as it controls over $392.64 million in net assets as of this date.

Despite its dominance in the XRP ETF market, Bitwise has remained muted all week, showing zero daily participation since November 9, when it posted its highest-ever daily outflow of $9.40 million.
