💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

According to recent reports, that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

Sources indicate that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's newly introduced private AI app, ZetaLabs, debuts alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a latest whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

It has been revealed that on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the blueprint, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain indicates it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain claims the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

According to recent reports, the biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange consumers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

It has been revealed that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain states it will announce any change to the process in advance.

Sources indicate that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

Industry observers note that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Sources indicate that taken together, this looks more like a retirement strategy for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Florida slashed property taxes. Now cities must cut services and ‘niceties’ like Christmas parades: ‘this is only the beginning of the vast reduction’

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cold reality of cutting local tax revenue by billions of dollars a year is starting to dawn on Floridians, who voted to slash property taxes earlier this month.
  • Recent findings suggest that amendment 3 expands the so-called homestead exemption, shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation.
  • It also lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% hike to 5%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cold reality of cutting local tax revenue by billions of dollars a year is starting to dawn on Floridians, who voted to slash property taxes earlier this month.

Recent findings suggest that amendment 3 expands the so-called homestead exemption, shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation. It will nearly triple from $51,400 right now to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028.

It also lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% hike to 5%. The amendment doesn’t apply to school-related property taxes but creates a path for abolishing non-school property taxes completely.

State economists have projected that local governments will lose nearly $5 billion in the first year and nearly $12 billion a year once the exemption is fully phased in.

It has been revealed that to be sure, local governments can raise revenue in other ways, such sales taxes and fees. Substantial cities can also rely more on taxes aimed at tourists, but smaller communities will be hit especially hard with some losing the bulk of their tax base.

Cities are now scrambling to figure out how to fund vital services like police, fire fighters and paramedics as well as roads and other infrastructure with much smaller budgets.

It has been revealed that in Deltona, City Manager Doc Dougherty told residents that the Christmas parade was canceled and blamed Amendment 3, warning that cuts wouldn’t end there. He estimated the city’s budget must be cut by $12 million in the coming year and then another $5 million the following year. By 2030, Deltona is expected to cut more than $23 million.

“Even though we have been doing everything right by reducing our tax millage for the past four years, including roll back this year, this is only the beginning of the vast reduction in Cityservices our residents will face for years to come,” Dougherty wrote in a letter to residents on Saturday.

According to recent reports, he added that all city events are effectively cancelled, except for two upcoming 5K runs that are self-supporting. Deltona is also withdrawing vehicle orders, terminating construction contracts, and cancelling professional services to “meet the goal of what was voted for by the residents.”.

Elsewhere in Florida, Delray Beach stopped funding its St. Patrick’s Day Parade, St. Petersburg is ending its beach trolley service, and Brevard County is targeting park maintenance, mosquito control, athletic fields, youth sports programs and playground repairs as areas for potential cuts.

Manatee County Commissioner George Kruse gave a similarly bleak assessment of the new revenue landscape. In a Substack post on Nov. 13, he estimated there will be $63 million less in tax revenue next year and $113 million less the following year.

While the state has endured past recessions and real estate crashes that shrank local tax revenue, Kruse pointed out that Amendment 3 is entirely different.

Sources indicate that “This isn’t a cycle, this is a permanent, structural shift in how government functions. Forever,” he wrote. “A facility that closes, will stay closed. An employee going part time, will never come back full time. A ‘delay’ in a capital project used to mean later, now it means never.”.

To close the massive revenue shortfall, Kruse said a “small fraction” could be covered by adjustments to fees, but the county sheriff must offer a material budget cut too.

He vowed to reject any latest sales taxes or higher property tax rates that put a heavier burden on renters and small businesses, while acknowledging that reductions in services will disproportionately affect those most in need of affordability.

“But last week, 65% of Manatee voters said they wanted to forego services and quality of life for lower property taxes,” Kruse added. “So that’s how this Board needs to cover this permanent gap.”.

He then went through a list of areas the county must scrutinize, including publicly owned assets, department consolidations, privatization, new infrastructure projects, special tax zones, interlocal agreement, funding for nonprofits, and even “niceties” that provide community spirit.

“That includes sponsorships, parades, movies in the park, holiday events,” Kruse explained. “Everything adds up when trying to fill such a large hole in the budget. We can’t layoff a needed employee while redirecting their salary to firework displays.”.

According to recent reports, amendment 3 may also require the county to rethink how it develops, such as favoring rental properties in denser areas over new homes in urban sprawl that entail added infrastructure costs, he noted. But throttling housing supply will raise home prices and rents, worsening the affordability issues that Amendment 3 is supposed to address.

According to recent reports, outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who backed Amendment 3, has dismissed such warnings as “fearmongering” and suggested state grants could offset any budget shortfalls to local agencies. Many details are lacking, and DeSantis has called for a special session of the legislature to spell out exactly how the amendment will work.

Recent findings suggest that but leaders in the state house have said a special session isn’t necessary, with Senate Majority Leader-designate Nick DiCeglie warning local governments against fee hikes. That means DeSantis’ successor, Governor-elect Byron Donalds, will be responsible for dealing with the fallout.

Despite the budget crunch local governments face, DeSantis also urged state lawmakers to block latest taxes and fees.

“There won’t be fee hikes if the Legislature stops it. Pass a taxpayer bill of rights, limit local spending and protect against newly introduced local taxes and fees,” he posted on X on Wednesday.
